title: DivCDSR: A Model-Agnostic Framework for Diverse Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation

problem.claim: Cross-domain sequential recommendation can improve accuracy while narrowing users' scope of interests and reducing recommendation diversity.

gap.claim: The effect of cross-domain sequential recommendation on recommendation diversity is largely unexplored.

contributions.claim: DivCDSR is a model-agnostic framework for enhancing diversity in cross-domain sequential recommendation.
A dual-prototype semantic constraint mechanism addresses homogenization through intra-domain clustering with orthogonalization and inter-domain separation.
A dual-guided diffusion module augments source-domain information by generating new sequences to address information asymmetry.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that they are the first to reveal that cross-domain sequential recommendation can improve accuracy at the cost of diversity.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report rigorous empirical experiments and theoretical analysis identifying domain homogeneity and information asymmetry as determinants of declining diversity.
Experiments on three public datasets reportedly show improved diversity metrics while maintaining or improving recommendation accuracy.
The authors report that all datasets and code are publicly available.

narrative_sequence.summary: Cross-domain sequential recommendation improves sparsity handling and accuracy, but its effect on diversity is largely unexplored.
The authors describe an accuracy–diversity tradeoff in which cross-domain recommendation can confine users to narrower interests.
The reported determinants of declining diversity are domain homogeneity and information asymmetry.
DivCDSR combines dual-prototype semantic constraints with dual-guided diffusion to address the two determinants.
Experiments on three public datasets reportedly improve diversity while maintaining or improving accuracy.

source_observation.claim: Cross-domain information can improve accuracy while reducing recommendation diversity when domains are overly homogeneous or source-domain signals are insufficient.

interpretation.claim: Cross-domain transfer should be evaluated for both utility and interest coverage rather than accuracy alone.

application.claim: Recommendation systems using cross-domain transfer could monitor diversity metrics and diagnose domain similarity and source-signal strength.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether these determinants or interventions generalize beyond the reported recommendation setting and datasets.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the three datasets.
Metric values, baselines, statistical results, and experimental settings are not provided.
The theoretical analysis and the mechanisms' implementation details are not specified.
